---
title: "minicondition"
---





The purpose of **minicondition** is to provide a zero-dependency
reimplementation of a small slice of the
[**rlang**](https://rlang.r-lib.org/) package: thin wrappers around
base R's own condition system that signal a *classed* condition,
catchable specifically by that class. The [README](https://github.com/djnavarro/minis/tree/main/minicondition)
provides the **rlang**-parity notes; this page focuses mostly on the
catch-by-class behaviour, since that's the main reason to reach for
**minicondition** over plain `stop()`/`warning()`/`message()`.

## Functions

The [**minicondition.R**](https://github.com/djnavarro/minis/blob/main/minicondition/minicondition.R)
script supplies four core functions:

- `.cond_abort(message, class = NULL)` is used to signal a classed
  error.
- `.cond_warn(message, class = NULL)` is used to signal a classed
  warning.
- `.cond_inform(message, class = NULL)` is used to signal a classed
  message.
- `.cond_assert(expr, message, class = NULL)` is used to call
  `.cond_abort()` if `expr` isn't entirely `TRUE`; `NA` counts as a
  failure.

There is also one internal helper:

- `.cond_condition()` builds the classed condition object that
  `.cond_abort()`/`_warn()`/`_inform()` each hand off to base
  `stop()`/`warning()`/`message()`.

## Why classes matter

A plain `stop("bad input")` produces a condition of class `c("simpleError", "error", "condition")` -- generic, and indistinguishable from any other error at the point where it's caught. That's fine for a one-off script, but it's a problem inside a package: callers who want to react to *this specific kind* of failure (retry, fall back to a default, show a custom message) have no reliable way to distinguish it from every other error your code might raise. The `.cond_abort()` function solves that by adding an extra class on
top of `"error"`, so `tryCatch()` can dispatch on it directly:



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tryCatch(
  .cond_abort("bad input", class = "mypkg_invalid_input"),
  mypkg_invalid_input = function(e) message("caught: ", conditionMessage(e))
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
caught: bad input
```


:::
:::



Note that `.cond_abort()` uses base `stop()` internally, not `rlang::abort()` -- but the mechanics of catching by class are identical either way. The `tryCatch()`/`withCallingHandlers()` functions dispatch on a
condition object's `class` attribute, regardless of what function
signalled it:



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
e <- tryCatch(.cond_abort("x", class = "mypkg_invalid_input"), error = function(e) e)
class(e)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "mypkg_invalid_input" "error"               "condition"          
```


:::
:::



## Unmatched handlers fall through; `error` still catches it

A handler for an unrelated class simply doesn't match -- `tryCatch()` tries each handler in order and uses the first one whose class matches. Since the condition is still, underneath the custom class, an ordinary `error` (see the `class(e)` output above), a generic `error` handler still catches it as a fallback if nothing more specific matches first:



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tryCatch(
  .cond_abort("bad input", class = "mypkg_invalid_input"),
  mypkg_other_class = function(e) message("this handler never runs"),
  error = function(e) message("caught generically as a plain error: ", conditionMessage(e))
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
caught generically as a plain error: bad input
```


:::
:::



This is the same layering `rlang` conditions use: a custom class sits *in addition to* the base `error`/`warning`/`message` class, not instead of it, so code that only knows about the generic type still works.

## Warnings and messages work the same way

The `.cond_warn()` function signals a classed warning, catchable via
`withCallingHandlers()` (warnings, unlike errors, don't unwind the
call stack, so catching them with `tryCatch()` would abandon whatever
code was about to run after the warning -- `withCallingHandlers()`
lets the handler run and then hand control back):



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
withCallingHandlers(
  .cond_warn("using a fallback default", class = "mypkg_fallback_used"),
  mypkg_fallback_used = function(w) {
    message("caught warning: ", conditionMessage(w))
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
caught warning: using a fallback default
```


:::
:::



The `invokeRestart("muffleWarning")` call suppresses the warning from also being printed by R's default warning handler -- without it, the warning would print a second time after the custom handler runs.

The `.cond_inform()` function signals a classed message -- uncaught,
it just prints like an ordinary `message()` call, since messages are
typically meant to be seen unless something specifically wants to
intercept them:



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
.cond_inform("starting up", class = "mypkg_startup")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
starting up
```


:::
:::



## `.cond_assert()`: abort if a condition doesn't hold

The `.cond_assert()` function is `.cond_abort()` plus a check: pass it
a logical expression, and it aborts (with the same classed-error
mechanics as above) only if that expression isn't entirely `TRUE`. A
passing assertion is silent, so it's safe to sprinkle through code as
a precondition check without cluttering normal output:



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
x <- 5
.cond_assert(x > 0, "x must be positive.")
```
:::



A failing one raises a classed error, catchable the same way as `.cond_abort()` -- which makes sense, since that's exactly what it calls internally:



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tryCatch(
  .cond_assert(x > 0 && x < 3, "x must be between 0 and 3.", class = "mypkg_range_error"),
  mypkg_range_error = function(e) message("caught: ", conditionMessage(e))
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
caught: x must be between 0 and 3.
```


:::
:::



## `NA` counts as a failure, not a crash

The `.cond_assert()` function accepts a vector, not just a single
logical value, and checks that *every* element is `TRUE`. That raises
a subtlety: what should happen if the vector contains `NA`? This is a
deliberate fix relative to the source this was adapted from: a naive
`if (any(expr == FALSE))` errors outright when `expr` contains `NA`
("missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed"), which would crash the
assertion check itself rather than raising the intended, informative
assertion error. It checks `anyNA(expr)` explicitly first instead, so
a vector containing `NA` fails the assertion cleanly, with the message
you asked for, instead of an unrelated low-level error:



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
y <- c(TRUE, TRUE, NA)
.cond_assert(y, "y must not contain NA.", class = "mypkg_na_error")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error:
! y must not contain NA.
```


:::
:::
